mcqs.question: Why is sizing a worker pool by job count alone (rather than by job type) usually the wrong approach?
options: Because job types can take wildly different amounts of worker time (e.g. milliseconds for a thumbnail vs seconds for a video rendition), so throughput per job type is what actually determines correct provisioning
Because job count is impossible to measure accurately in a queue-based system
Because all job types always take the exact same amount of worker time in practice
Because worker pools can only process one job type at a time regardless of configuration
mcqs.explanation: A worker pool sized on raw job count assumes uniform cost per job, but a thumbnail and a video rendition can differ by 40x in worker-seconds — provisioning has to account for that per job type. Job count is easy to measure; job types clearly differ in cost, which is the whole point; and worker pools can absolutely be configured per job type.

mcqs.question: What does giving each job attempt a deterministic idempotency key (like mediaId + jobType + version) actually protect against?
options: It prevents any job from ever failing in the first place
It removes the need for a job-state table entirely
A retried job overwrites or no-ops against the same output location instead of producing duplicate output or a duplicate completion notification
It guarantees every job completes in under one second
mcqs.explanation: The idempotency key ties output location and job identity to a stable value, so a retry lands on the same output and doesn't create a duplicate — that's the actual protection. It doesn't prevent failures (retries still happen), doesn't remove the need for a state table (which is still the source of truth for completion), and has no bearing on job runtime.

mcqs.question: Thumbnails and 4K video transcodes share one queue and worker pool. A burst of 4K jobs arrives. What happens to thumbnail requests, and what's the fix?
options: Thumbnails fail outright and must be resubmitted by the client
Nothing changes — job type has no effect on queue behavior
The worker pool automatically reorders jobs by expected duration with no configuration needed
Thumbnails wait behind the expensive jobs occupying every worker; the fix is separate queues and worker pools (or reserved capacity) per job type
mcqs.explanation: Sharing a queue means a burst of expensive jobs can occupy every worker, leaving cheap, near-instant jobs waiting — the fix is isolating job types into separate queues or worker pools so one type's cost profile can't block another. Thumbnails don't fail outright, they just wait; job type absolutely affects queue behavior when pools are shared; and no built-in reordering happens without deliberately building it.

mcqs.question: A job fails partway through after already writing some output, and the system retries it from scratch with no idempotency key. What's the realistic consequence?
options: The retry always fails instantly with no side effects
The system automatically detects and merges the duplicate output with no extra design needed
It silently duplicates stored output and can fire a second completion callback to the caller, unnoticed until storage costs or downstream duplicate-processing show up
Nothing — retrying a job with no idempotency key is always perfectly safe
mcqs.explanation: Without a stable identity for the job's output, a retry after partial success writes a new copy under a different path or ID and can notify the caller again — quietly duplicating storage and downstream work. Retries don't fail instantly by default, there's no automatic dedup without deliberately building an idempotency key, and 'always safe' is precisely the wrong belief this pitfall calls out.
